items.question: What did you learn from trying neural operators for weather modeling?
items.object: Neural operators for weather modeling
items.answer: We set out looking for interesting examples, and one of them was weather modeling because the weather data is open source. Given that the data was there, we were like, okay, let's just go try it. That's the beauty of it: whenever data is available, it's really good news. A lot of weather scientists did caution us back then, this was back in '21, and they said, no, no, this is so difficult. There have been decades of development in traditional weather forecasting, and that's very careful bottom-up, physics-based modeling. Assuming, oh, this is the fluid dynamics, can you go predict the weather the next day, and so on? A lot of the thinking was that AI is just not going to be able to beat the decades of work in weather modeling. But to our surprise, we just went ahead, we trained them, we used neural operators to effectively capture the phenomena, and we found that it's not only accurate, it's almost as close as traditional weather models, but also tens of thousands of times faster. What would take a big supercomputer to run can now be run, and we only needed a consumer-grade GPU. It was a small model, it fit very well, it's very fast, and it's accurate. I think that just changed everybody's thinking.

items.question: How do you think about the central challenge of bringing AI and science together?
items.object: Bringing AI and science together through physical modeling and formal verification
items.answer: To me, broadly, my thesis is AI and science: how we bring that together. When I started at Caltech almost a decade ago, my passion was always science, physics, but I was doing AI, so how to bring that together was where the first foundations got laid. There are several aspects to that. People have been thinking how to use language models for science. You can do a lot of hypothesis generation, you can have ideas, but ideas are not enough. The bottleneck is going and testing and verifying that they work in the real world. This is where a lot of my recent focus has been: how do we ensure that we can build AI that has guarantees that it will work in the physical world or scientific domains? One way to think about it is, can we model and keep the physics correct? That's where neural operators come in. The other aspect is, can we verify symbolically certain aspects? If we claim that a theorem is correct, we have to verify that. That's where Lean as a formal language can be useful for verification. How do we bring that together with language models is where a lot of mathematical reasoning has been at the forefront.

items.object: TorchLean and verification of neural networks in control loops
items.answer: TorchLean is in that realm where we say not only do you want to verify mathematical statements, you may want to verify what neural networks themselves claim to deliver. items.question: How do you think about the kinds of guarantees TorchLean can provide for neural networks?

items.answer: The natural one is certified robustness: if your inputs are perturbed by a certain amount, how much is the output going to be perturbed? This sensitivity analysis is another term. Having those kinds of bounds for different architectures can help us not only train neural networks to do well in a control loop, but also worry about safety, robustness, and stability. That's one example of an application. More broadly, you need verification in lots of scenarios that involve neural networks. Control loops are one. Another example is using physics-informed neural networks to solve partial differential equations or come up with systems guaranteed to satisfy certain physical laws. We also want to verify, for instance, that our neural network is only trained in finite precision. Can we overcome those requirements, and what are the shortcomings because we are using finite precision? Can we also bound those? Those are other kinds of bounds that work in TorchLean. All aspects of the effect of precision, the effect of perturbation, we can have algorithms implemented in Lean.

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of physics-informed neural networks for time-dependent problems?
items.object: Physics-informed neural networks and their optimization limits
items.answer: Physics informed neural nets are about saying, I write down a PDE, a partial differential equation, and hopefully the optimization succeeds and I get the answer, right? Of course, if optimization was not at all an issue, this would be universal. You solve everything; we're all happy. But that's not the case. Optimization ends up being usually very difficult, especially for problems that are time dependent, meaning it's not just stationary, you also have time. The time component in many cases could be turbulent, like in the case of fluid dynamics. If you run it long enough, it can become chaotic. Very small fine scale effects matter. In those cases, just trying to solve a partial differential equation at all times is just hopeless. This is not an optimization landscape that I think we can have any handle on, and this is where the idea that from scratch we would be able to solve these equations using a neural net is not possible.

We don't just solve equations and have synthetic data, but we also have real data by observing the weather. Why not make use of all of the data available? items.question: Why do you see neural operators as a useful generalization of standard neural networks for modeling the physical world?
items.object: Neural operators as a generalization of neural networks for multiscale physical data
items.answer:
With neural operators, we're learning on data, the same as neural networks. But the difference is neural operators, you can think of them as a generalization of neural networks. With standard neural networks, the inputs and outputs are of fixed size. In language we have fixed vocabulary; we fix what the input and output are. Same with images in computer vision, and in videos we assume a fixed resolution. Our inputs and outputs are always at that fixed resolution; we can't change it post hoc.

With a lot of this physical data, the idea is our world is inherently multiscale, so you should not be deciding beforehand what the resolution is. Maybe you have weather data available only at coarse resolution, but really the actual phenomena is happening at a finer scale. Maybe you want to after that incorporate either additional data at finer resolution or add in physical constraints at finer resolution. We should have that flexibility and think of the world not at these fixed resolutions, but as one that's happening infinitely. The real world happens at that infinite resolution, and that's what neural operators enable, because they model inputs and outputs as continuous functions that can be infinitely resolved, that can have infinite discretization. At inference time, you can give it inputs and ask for outputs at any resolution, so you're not just limited to the resolution of training that we see in standard neural networks. That's what neural operators enable, so neural operators enable us to zoom in and out as we like.

items.question: How do you think about making neural operators predict at a higher resolution than their training data?
items.object: Zero-shot super-resolution and physics-informed neural operators
items.answer: If you're asking about making predictions at a higher resolution than what's seen, what we call zero shot super resolution, you're kind of making some guesses. That's what these models are doing: they're trying to regularize and smoothly extend to higher resolution. But of course, if you now give the model additional information in terms of, let's say, a physical loss, so you could give it partial differential equation constraints, conservation laws, and you can now enforce them at a finer resolution than the data you have, then there's more guidance. That way it can come up with the right answers even at higher resolution because you're giving it constraints at higher resolution. That's how we can ensure that these physics informed neural operators can work at higher fidelity and higher resolution than even the training data that was available.

items.question: Why do you see Fourier neural operators as an effective architecture for modeling natural phenomena?
items.object: Fourier neural operators
items.answer:
What I mentioned is, neural operators as a class of models allow us to have any resolution input and any resolution output, and learn the mapping between them. That's really called an operator, the mapping between function spaces. That's the reasoning behind the name neural operator. A Fourier neural operator was one of the early setups or architectures we came up with, and the reason why that's been so successful is because it strikes a nice trade off between efficiency and expressivity.

The Fourier space allows us to capture non-local phenomena. Something that's non-local in the Fourier domain could be efficiently captured. A lot of phenomena we see in nature, whether it's fluid dynamics, material deformation, quantum chemistry, a lot of them are non-local. The differential equation, like the derivative, is local, but the inverse of it is essentially integration; it's non-local. The solutions are non-local, and these models are able to capture that. At the same time, doing a Fourier transform is efficient, and it nicely captures a lot of inductive bias we see in many of these natural phenomena. But this doesn't mean that we're capturing the world entirely in the Fourier basis. It's not a linear representation in the Fourier basis, which is what classical numerical methods do. We add non-linearity, just as a transformer and other neural nets, in between Fourier layers, and we also add residual connections. All of these architectural aspects inspired by other neural nets that work well, bringing that together really helps us get the best of both worlds.

If we were to use transformers and require a very high resolution, it would become untenable because of the quadratic complexity and all to all connections. On the other hand, with Fourier transforms we have quasi-linear complexity, and still we have global connections in a way. We can model these non-local phenomena.

items.question: What did your experience applying neural operators to weather forecasting teach you about their potential?
items.object: Neural operators for weather forecasting
items.answer:
For us, when we started with neural operators for partial differential equations, but also more broadly, you don't even need to assume they're partial differential equations. It could be any spatiotemporal or data at multiple scales. We set out looking for interesting examples, and one of them was weather modeling, because the weather data is open source. It's available, called ERA5, from the ECMWF, the European Agency for Global Weather Modeling. Given that the data was there, we were like, okay, let's just go try it. That's the beauty of it: whenever data is available, it's really good news.

A lot of weather scientists did caution us back then, this was back in 2021, and they said, "No, no, no, this is so difficult. There have been decades of development in traditional weather forecasting," and that's very careful bottom up physics based modeling, assuming this is fluid dynamics, can you predict the weather the next day, and so on. A lot of the thinking was that AI is just not going to be able to beat the decades of work in weather modeling. But to our surprise, we went ahead, trained them, used neural operators to effectively capture the phenomena. We found that it's not only accurate, it's almost as close to what the traditional weather models can do, but also tens of thousands of times faster. What would take a big supercomputer to run can now be run with a consumer grade GPU. It was a small model, it fit very well, it's very fast and it's accurate.

I think that just changed everybody's thinking after that. DeepMind, Huawei, many others followed us a year later and released their own models. We were the first to open source our weather model, ForecastNet, and do it permissively. That's what allowed companies, weather agencies, everybody to build on us. It's been a really interesting revolution to see that the weather models are now out there, weather agencies are adopting them.

items.question: What do you expect from a foundation model for weather and climate?
items.object: Foundation models for weather and climate
items.answer:
There's the aspect that there is short term weather, what is predictable for the next two weeks, and then there's the long term, going to subseasonal to ultimately climate modeling. Traditionally what people did was to have different models for these different scenarios. There's a different kind of system that works for short term, another system works for long term. To me, there's only one Earth. If you want a foundation model, if the claim is that it should be able to do both very short term as well as very long term together, that's where in ForecastNet 3, the latest iteration of the model, we're able to do both.

That's because you also incorporate the spherical geometry of the Earth. With a lot of the architectures that have been getting fairly good accuracies for short term weather, when you run them for longer term, several months to even a year, even before that it just very quickly blows up, because it assumes the world is a rectangle, which it isn't. Incorporating all of the geometry and that information into neural operators means that we can faithfully run the same model also longer term and make this into a climate model. This is where the Allen AI Institute has now built climate models based on our neural operator architecture, and that's the only one that works as an AI emulator. None of the other architectures work for climate, because climate requires us to assume the world is a globe, and if you are repeatedly rolling out, you kind of keep that information. Whereas if it's like a narrow surrogate, that's what I consider a weather model. You just narrowly look at a few metrics.

items.question: How do you see the role of theoretical foundations in your work changing as AI has developed?
items.object: The changing role of theoretical foundations in AI research
items.answer:
To me, I feel like I've grown along with AI. When AI was in this phase where neural nets were not working because there wasn't enough data and all kinds of other reasons, you kind of have to build the theoretical foundations and hope that leads you to a place where you get algorithms to work.

Back then, tensor methods were with that idea: pre deep learning, we still wanted structure. We had probabilistic models like latent Dirichlet allocation for topic modeling, and solving those was hard, but tensor methods gave us a way to be very practical. It's parallel and can be done at large scale, but still has a nice theoretical basis.

As deep learning started taking off, we could see that it works well in practice. There is a little bit of theoretical understanding, but not a whole lot because of how complex it is. To me, theory should not be a constraint; it should be an aid. A lot of the exploration was to make this work well in practice. Then I went to Amazon Web Services, then NVIDIA, really making things work at scale and getting hands dirty.

Now I see a full circle, because a lot of purely data driven approaches are seeing saturation. We want to ask: can we make them much more energy efficient or hardware efficient? That's one aspect. The other is areas like this where in the physical world we don't have enough data, we're asking for hard extrapolation. Discovery by nature is about extrapolation; we will never have data about a new discovery. That's my definition. There we need to go back to thinking in principled ways, whether it's architecture design, algorithm design, or the right loss functions. We need to be much more mindful.

items.question: How do you see AI-driven inverse design advancing innovation in physical systems?

items.answer:
We're looking at designing the mask for inverse lithography, meaning now there's an inverse design problem. We're also able to do that for designing gates in quantum dots, nonlinear photonics. What is common is the idea that there's a forward model simulating the physics, but now we want the inverse design problem: we can optimize the best design. Humans are usually not good at looking at highly nonlinear phenomena and saying maybe this combination of all these gates coming together helps pull the electrons together in a quantum gate. Our collaborators were struggling to do that manually, and with AI we're now able to come up with very efficient designs, but also those we know actually work because we have the simulation as part of the loop saying that they work well.

These are examples where it's not just about simulation; it's about novel designs and novel discoveries that enable us to move the needle of innovation itself.
